lines: This is a few seconds of a volleyball match.
As humans, we see straight away what is happening: the left team is attacking, with a spike.
The goal of this project is to teach a computer to understand that, automatically, from the video.
This task is called group activity recognition: not what one person does, but what the whole team does.
It is useful for sports analytics, for automatic highlights, and for coaching.
In volleyball, there are eight team activities: a set, a spike, a pass, or winning the point, for the left or for the right team.
To solve it, I started from a well-known paper.
A Hierarchical Deep Temporal Model for Group Activity Recognition, by Mostafa Ibrahim and his colleagues, published at CVPR in 2016.
It introduced the Volleyball dataset, which is still a reference for this problem today.
My work follows three phases.
First, I reimplemented the paper, as faithfully as possible.
Second, I modernized it, following the course of the paper's author.
And third, I replaced the architecture with my own design.
Before building any model, I studied the data.
Fifty-five matches, and four thousand eight hundred clips. In every clip, the twelve players have a box, and a label saying what they do.
Most players are simply standing, so the important actions, like a spike or a set, are rare.
I also measured what these labels can tell us.
Knowing what each player does, the kind of activity is ninety-four percent predictable.
But left or right is a coin flip, unless the two teams are kept apart. Then it jumps to eighty-nine percent. Keep this in mind, it comes back later.
Here is the model of the paper. This figure comes from the paper itself.
Each player is cropped from the image, and a convolutional network describes what he looks like.
A first LSTM follows each player over time, to understand his action.
Then all the players are pooled together, into one description of the scene.
And a second LSTM follows the scene over time, to decide the team activity.
Phase one. I rewrote this model in PyTorch, with the same AlexNet network and the same training protocol.
My reproduction reaches eighty-five point nine percent, where the paper reports eighty-one point nine.
And every conclusion of the paper is confirmed, which validates my implementation.
Phase two. I modernized the pipeline.
I replaced AlexNet with ResNet50, kept the full wide frame, and added mirrored training images.
Then I rebuilt the eight baselines of the course, step by step, from a simple image classifier to the full model.
Every baseline improves, by seven to nineteen points over the paper.
The most important change is this one.
Instead of mixing the twelve players together, they are split into the left team and the right team, and each team gets its own summary.
This single idea takes the model from seventy-eight to almost ninety-two percent. Exactly what the data analysis predicted.
Phase three. I replaced the architecture itself.
Instead of two LSTMs and a pooling, I use a transformer.
Every player, at every moment, becomes a token, and each token can look at all the others. This is called attention.
And instead of training in two separate stages, the whole network learns at once, with two goals: each player's action, and the team activity.
This new design reaches ninety-two point seven percent.
I then tuned it with Optuna, averaged each clip with its mirror image, and combined several models.
The final accuracy is ninety-three point nine percent, on matches the model has never seen.
One question remained. In a real video, nobody gives us the boxes of the players.
So I tested nine object detectors, from YOLO to Faster R-CNN, and measured how my model works with each of them.
Off the shelf, they also detect referees and line judges, and they miss players in unusual poses.
So I fine-tuned YOLO on the players. It now finds ninety-six percent of them, at almost forty frames per second.
And from the raw video, without a single annotated box, the system still reaches ninety-two point three percent.
Here is the complete system, on a full rally from a match it has never seen.
It finds the players, recognizes what each one does, splits the two teams, and the bars show its decision, frame after frame.
To sum up: I reproduced the paper, improved it by ten points, and designed my own architecture, which reaches ninety-three point nine percent.
Three lessons. Keep the teams apart. Train the whole network end to end. And use simple tricks, like test-time augmentation.
Thank you for watching. The code and all the results are on GitHub.
